title: Trace Cache over Conventional Instruction Cache
decision: Adopted an Execution Trace Cache that stores decoded micro-ops (uops) in the dynamic execution path, rather than a conventional L1 instruction cache storing x86 instructions.
alternatives_or_rejected: The paper contrasts this with a traditional instruction cache that would require decoding each time. The trace cache stores already-decoded uops, effectively replacing the L1 I-cache.
rationale: The Pentium 4 can execute instructions faster than it can decode them; the trace cache bypasses the decoder on cache hits, increasing front-end bandwidth.
outcome: A 12K uop trace cache that delivers up to 6 uops per cycle to the execution engine.
quote_as_recalled: The decoder can decode only one IA32 instruction per cycle. However, the decoded instructions are cached in the trace cache.
weakest_point: The exact microarchitecture details (e.g., 12K uop size) are from secondary sources, not directly verified from the paper text.

title: Deep Pipelining / Hyper Pipelined Technology
decision: Implemented a very deep pipeline (20 stages) to achieve high clock frequencies, significantly deeper than the P6 family.
alternatives_or_rejected: The paper implies a trade-off against the shorter pipeline of the P6 architecture, choosing frequency over instructions-per-clock (IPC) for the initial NetBurst implementation.
rationale: To achieve industry-leading clock rates (starting at 1.5 GHz) and deliver a substantial performance gain for key applications.
outcome: The Pentium 4 achieved a 1.5 GHz clock frequency at introduction, with a 20-stage pipeline.
weakest_point: The exact pipeline stage count (20) is a well-known fact but may not be explicitly emphasized as a 'decision' with trade-offs in the paper.

title: Double-Pumped (2x Core Frequency) ALU
decision: Designed a double-pumped Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) that operates at twice the core processor frequency.
rationale: To execute simple integer instructions at extremely low latency, effectively allowing them to run at 2x the core clock speed.
outcome: An ALU running at 3 GHz (on a 1.5 GHz core) that handles simple integer operations, forming the Rapid Execution Engine.
quote_as_recalled: the extremely low latency double-pumped Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) that runs at 3GHz.
weakest_point: The specific frequency (3 GHz) is from the abstract; the paper likely mentions it, but the exact phrasing might differ.

title: Low-Latency Level 1 Data Cache (2-cycle access)
decision: Implemented a very low latency Level 1 data cache that can be accessed in just two clock cycles.
rationale: To feed the high-speed execution engine with data quickly and maintain performance despite the deep pipeline.
outcome: A low-latency L1 data cache that supports the Rapid Execution Engine's high throughput.
quote_as_recalled: the very low latency Level 1 data cache that is accessed in just two clock cycles.
weakest_point: The cache size (8KB) is not mentioned in the abstract; this detail is from general knowledge and may not be in the paper.

title: Rapid Execution Engine with ALUs at 2x Core Frequency
where_in_paper: Out-of-order execution engine / Rapid Execution Engine section
decision: Created the Rapid Execution Engine where the Arithmetic Logic Units (ALUs) run at twice the core frequency.
rationale: To allow frequently used integer instructions to execute at double the core clock, improving performance.
outcome: Two ALUs running at double the processor frequency, enabling high-speed integer execution.
quote_as_recalled: Arithmetic Logic Units (ALUs) run at twice the processor frequency.
weakest_point: This is closely related to the 'Double-Pumped ALU' decision; the paper might present them as the same feature.
